6. Approval, licensing and registration of factories.
(1) The State Government may make rules requiring, for the purposes of this Act, the submission of plans of any class or description of factories to the Chief Inspector or the Inspector.
(2) Where the occupier or owner of a factory proposes to use any premises as a factory, he shall submit to the Chief Inspector or Inspector, as required by the rules, the plans of the factory for approval.
(3) The Chief Inspector or the Inspector shall grant a certificate of approval if the plans submitted are in conformity with the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder.
(4) If within three months from the date of submission of plans, no order is communicated to the applicant, the plans shall be deemed to have been approved and the applicant shall be entitled to proceed with the construction or extension of the factory in conformity with such plans.

Section 6 — Approval of Factories (Simple Explanation)

What does this section say?
Before building or using premises as a factory, the owner must submit building plans to the government inspector.

The inspector checks:
• Do the plans follow all Factories Act rules?
• Are safety, health, and welfare requirements met?

Three possible outcomes:
1. Approved → Inspector gives a certificate. You can build.
2. Rejected → Plans don't meet requirements. You must revise.
3. Deemed Approval → Most important concept here.

Deemed Approval (subsection 4):
If the government inspector does NOT respond within 3 months from submission, the plans are automatically considered approved — even without any formal certificate.

Why this matters:
This protects factory owners from bureaucratic delays. If the government is slow to act, the owner has legal protection to proceed with construction as if approval was granted.

In practice:
Many factories use this provision when dealing with slow government processing. After 3 months of silence, they have legal cover to move forward.

Code on Wages — Key Definitions (Simple Explanation)

1. Employer
An employer is any person who hires one or more workers — directly or through a contractor.
Even if workers are hired through a middleman (contractor), the main company can still be the "employer" under this Code.

2. Wages — What is Included
Wages = all money you receive for working, including:
• Basic pay (your base salary)
• Dearness Allowance (DA — inflation adjustment)
• Retaining allowance (paid to keep skilled workers even during off-seasons)

3. Wages — What is NOT Included
The following are NOT counted as wages:
• Performance bonuses not contractually guaranteed
• Free housing, electricity, water, medical treatment provided by employer
• Travel/expense reimbursements for job-specific travel
• Gratuity (the lump sum paid when you leave after long service)

Remuneration in Kind:
If your employer pays part of your compensation in goods or services instead of cash (e.g., free canteen food, company accommodation), the monetary value of those goods/services counts toward wages under this Code.

Why this definition matters:
Employers sometimes try to give non-cash benefits to reduce declared wages (and lower their PF/ESI obligations). This definition prevents that by including most regular compensation.

Section 13 Highlighted Part — Proviso (Simple Explanation)

Main rule: Wages must be paid in full — no deductions allowed unless specifically permitted by this Code.

The Highlighted Proviso explains what does NOT count as a "deduction":

If an employer punishes a worker for genuine misconduct using these disciplinary actions:
(i) Withholding increment or promotion — e.g., you don't get your annual raise because of poor performance
(ii) Reduction in rank or pay scale — e.g., demoted from Senior to Junior due to disciplinary issue
(iii) Suspension — temporary removal from work

→ The resulting loss of wages is NOT considered an illegal deduction.

Why this matters:
Without this exception, any disciplinary action that results in lower pay could be challenged as an unauthorized deduction. The proviso clarifies that legitimate disciplinary pay-cuts are allowed, as long as there is "good and sufficient cause".

Key condition: "good and sufficient cause" — the employer cannot arbitrarily withhold pay. There must be a genuine, documented reason. Workers can challenge disciplinary actions if the cause was not genuine.

Section 9 — Canteens for Motor Transport Workers (Simple Explanation)

Main Rule:
If a transport company employs more than the prescribed number of motor transport workers (set by the State Government), they MUST provide and maintain a canteen.

Who are motor transport workers?
Drivers, conductors, cleaners, mechanics — anyone employed in a motor transport undertaking.

What the Government can regulate (subsection 2):
(a) When canteen must be ready — deadline date
(b) Physical standards — construction, furniture, space requirements
(c) Food and prices — what items must be available, maximum prices charged
(d) Management committee — workers must have representation in how the canteen is run (not just employer control)

Why this provision exists:
Motor transport workers often travel long routes and irregular hours. Unlike factory workers who stay at one location, transport workers cannot easily find food. Providing regulated, subsidized canteen facilities at depots/yards is essential.

Connection to Wages (Remuneration in Kind):
If the employer provides free meals at the canteen as part of the employment contract, the market value of those meals counts as wages under the Code on Wages — this prevents employers from replacing cash wages with food benefits to reduce formal wage liability.
